awd_titl_txt: RI: Small: Cooperative Planning and Learning via Scalable and Learnable Multi-Agent Commitments
awd_abstract_narration:
Stemming from human societies, the notion of commitment refers to a decision maker, or agent, making credible and prolonged promises about various aspects of the consequences of its future decisions, thus facilitating cooperation with other agents. Engineering commitments is therefore a promising framework to achieve cooperative artificial intelligence (AI) that equips a group of autonomous agents with the capability of planning and learning to maximize their joint utility. This research project seeks to initiate a paradigm shift that brings the notion of commitment to its full potential by scaling it to various dimensions of complexity in cooperative AI, developing novel methods that promise to significantly and positively impact real-world and large-scale cooperative AI applications. This project integrates an array of education initiatives, playing key roles in PI's classes, the recruitment and training of undergraduate students from underrepresented backgrounds, and extensive activities planned to involve high school students and junior researchers.

This research consists of two cohesive thrusts: Thrust 1 redesigns an existing approach for commitment-based distributed cooperative planning with a predefined parameterization for probabilistic commitments, by developing novel algorithms and analyses in planning under constraints and uncertainty, approximate linear programming, and robust planning that address long decision horizon and high-dimensional perception and action; Thrust 2 develops and evaluates a novel approach for distributed cooperative learning with emergent commitment parameterization, which combines the best from the framework of multi-agent commitments and deep reinforcement learning to address all aforementioned dimensions of complexity. Success of the proposed research is expected to significantly increase the applicability of commitment-based planning and learning for large-scale and complex cooperative AI systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
When multiple people work together on a task, say, merging onto a busy highway or coordinating a team project, they often make promises about what they will do next so that others can plan accordingly. This project brought the same idea, called commitment, to groups of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that must cooperate to solve complex problems. The central question was: how can AI agents make, communicate, and follow through on commitments to one another so they coordinate more effectively, even as the number of agents, the complexity of the environment, and the length of the task all grow?


Over the life of this award the team made research advances along two complementary directions.


The first direction aimed to scale commitments through structured policies. The team introduced a framework that uses Bayesian networks, a graphical form of probabilistic models, to represent how agents' decisions depend on one another. This allowed a smooth tradeoff between fully independent decision-making, which is simple but ignores coordination, and fully joint decision-making, which captures coordination but becomes computationally intractable with many agents. The team proved mathematical guarantees that policy-improvement algorithms converge under these structured policies, and showed that organizing agents into subteams yields convergence rates that depend only on subteam size rather than on the total number of agents. A follow-up study established that natural policy gradient methods applied to these Bayesian-network policies converge to near-optimal solutions, and introduced a novel regularization technique that maintains sufficient exploration throughout training.


The other direction aimed to learn effective commitments with world models and language. To move beyond settings where the environment dynamics are already known, the team developed methods for agents to learn their own predictive models of the world in a decentralized fashion, sharing only the most important information with one another under strict communication budgets. Remarkably, this selective-sharing approach sometimes outperformed methods that share everything, demonstrating that smart communication can substitute for brute-force centralization. The team also explored how large language models can serve as high-level planners: a framework called Tree of Options lets a language model reason about temporally extended actions expressed in natural language, plan sequences of such actions with Monte Carlo tree search, and then execute each step by generating code. On long-horizon tasks in a Minecraft environment, Tree of Options achieved higher success rates and better efficiency than existing approaches. These results were published at RLC 2025, ICLR 2026 workshops, and in Transactions on Machine Learning Research.


The team also studied when and why a simple "take turns improving" commitment strategy, known as best-response dynamics, leads agents to high-quality cooperative outcomes in Markov potential games. The analysis showed that alternating updates can match or exceed simultaneous updates for finding near-optimal solutions, an insight that proved powerful in practice: minimal modifications to existing decentralized deep reinforcement learning algorithms produced significant performance gains on standard benchmarks.


The project produced over ten peer-reviewed publications at venues including ICML, ICLR, RLC, TMLR, the Artificial Intelligence Journal, and several workshops at NeurIPS, CoRL, and IROS, making the methods and findings widely available to the research community.


Beyond PI’s research labs, the project supported the training of multiple PhD students who led individual research activities and published first-author papers at premier AI conferences. One research associate applied the commitment framework to autonomous driving, and an undergraduate student gained formative research experience in the PI's lab. Research outcomes were integrated into the PI's courses on optimization, multi-agent decision making, and advanced programming at PI’s current and former institutions. The project also informed the development of a new undergraduate course on multi-agent systems designed to bring current AI topics to a broader student audience.
